title: Technical notes
text:
Processing decisions

Streaming the LiDAR. The point cloud is far larger than the available disk, so each tile is downloaded, rasterised and deleted in turn. The horizontal coordinates are used as they are; the datum difference is about 1 m and matches the vector layers.
Roof holes. Dark or glassy roofs return no points, and filling them from the ground would make buildings disappear. Holes inside a footprint take the median height of the same building; buildings with less than 20% valid pixels use the recorded height.
Spikes and outliers. Isolated high returns (fewer than 2 neighbours within 10 m in a 5 × 5 window) are removed, and anything more than 400 m above the ground is treated as noise; one stray return near the TV masts otherwise cast kilometre-long shadows.
Holes outside buildings. Over water the surface takes the ground height; other holes are interpolated up to 10 px and otherwise take the ground, so river surfaces do not grow false structures.
Ground under bridges. Ground gaps are filled first from NOAA’s bare-earth model (bridges removed) and only then by interpolation, so bridge decks stay above the ground instead of being merged with it.
Leaf-off LiDAR. The survey was flown in March, so canopies have gaps. Inside the 2018 canopy mask, pixels below 2 m take the median of taller pixels in a 3 × 3 m window; a maximum filter was rejected because it raised the median tree height by about 5 m.
Trees outside the city. The land-cover layer stops at the city limit, so trees in the 1 km buffer come from CHMv2 (≥ 2 m); they only cast shadows onto city sidewalks.
Structures without footprints. Bridges and rail viaducts are kept as structures: areas at least 3 m high outside footprints and the canopy, cut where the surface jumps by more than 2 m, and kept if a piece covers at least 50 m² with a height spread of at most 3 m. Parked trains can pass this test too.
Flat-roof extrusion. Footprints with almost no LiDAR height (median below 2 m) but a recorded height of at least 3 m are built after the survey; they are extruded to the recorded height. Footprints where 30%–50% of pixels are tall overlap a neighbour and are skipped. In University City every extruded building was checked on 2025 aerial photos.
Bridge decks. A sidewalk segment is on a bridge when at least 80% of it lies within 15 m of an OSM road bridge and the two run within 20° of each other; its observer then stands on the deck. A plain intersection test would put every underpass on the bridge above it.
Terrain shadows. Bare ground also blocks the sun, which matters in steep valleys such as the Wissahickon at low sun.
Covered walkways. OpenStreetMap covered walkways and passages through buildings are added and counted as building shade at every hour.
Cost function kept as published. The coolest path sometimes has more sun than the shortest, when it trades tree shade for building shade (0.8% of test walks). The cost was kept unchanged, and the weighted exposure C is reported next to the sun share.
Which stops. Using every stop gave a median walk of 113 m, too short for any choice of route. Rapid transit plus frequent buses gives a median of 407 m and still reaches 82% of homes within 1.2 km.
Threshold for no cooler option. Sun reduction has a spike at exactly 0 (the coolest walk is the shortest) and is continuous from about 2% on, so the cut is placed where the spike ends.
Clusters. Clustering uses only 300–800 m walks so that cells are compared at the same walk length. Silhouette scores for k = 3–6 are 0.33–0.35, so k = 3 is a summary of a continuum rather than natural types.
Campus footways. The regional sidewalk data lack most campus paths, so University City adds OpenStreetMap footways (36 km), leaving out sidewalks, crossings, private and indoor ways. Each mapped entrance is linked to the nearest sidewalk point without crossing a building; links over 30 m were checked by hand and the ones that are not walkable removed.
Indoor baseline. In the indoor scenarios the shortest walk is always the outdoor one, so every scenario is compared against the same baseline.

title: Technical notes
text:
Validation

Synthetic shadows. Unit tests cast shadows from box buildings and trees on flat ground and check the shadow length against height / tan(sun elevation) for several sun positions, no shadow on the sunny side, tree versus building priority, terrain shadows and observers on bridge decks.
Building heights. LiDAR heights agree with the city’s recorded heights for 541,222 buildings (Spearman ρ = 0.84; Pearson r = 0.83). The median difference (LiDAR minus record) is −0.5 m, so LiDAR heights are typically 0.5 m lower than the records; the median absolute difference is 0.5 m.
Routing. With θ fixed, the search reproduces networkx Dijkstra exactly on 9,094 nodes (largest absolute difference 0). Hand-computed small networks check the cost rule, tree versus building shade and the indoor term.
Browser and analysis agree. The route tool’s JavaScript router returns the same shortest and coolest paths as the Python analysis for 100 random walks, scenarios and hours.
Direction of travel. Reversing 500 walks of at least 400 m (home → stop) changes little: mean sun reduction 14.2% one way and 14.2% the other, correlation 0.99.
Visual checks. The five rapid-transit stations with the largest sun reduction were checked route by route on aerial photos, as were the University City entrances and passages.

title: Methods
text:
Heights. The 2022 LiDAR survey gives the height of the ground, every building and every tree at 1 m.
Shadows. For 24 sun positions (June 21 and August 1, 8:00–19:00), we look from a point every 2 m along each sidewalk towards the sun. The point is in building shade if a building, bridge or the terrain is in the way, in tree shade if only trees are, and otherwise in the sun.
Sidewalks. Each stretch of sidewalk gets its metres of sun, tree shade and building shade for every hour.
Routes. For every walk we find two routes: the shortest, and the coolest, which has the lowest shade-weighted cost below.

title: Methods
section: The cost of a sunny metre
text:
The cost of a sunny metre
We use the cost function of Wen et al. (2025):
\[C = L_{\text{sun}} + (1 - 0.5\,\theta)\,L_{\text{tree}} + (1 - \theta)\,L_{\text{building}} + (1 - 1.5\,\theta)\,L_{\text{indoor}}\]
A metre in the sun costs 1. A metre in tree shade costs a little less (1 − 0.5θ), a metre in building shade less again (1 − θ), and an air-conditioned indoor metre the least (1 − 1.5θ): tree shade sits between sun and building shade. The reward θ grows with the distance already walked, so shade matters more the longer you have been in the heat:





θ as a function of distance already walked.




Because θ stays near 0.2 for the first 500 m, a short walk only takes a cooler route when it costs almost no extra distance.

title: Methods
text:
Walks home from transit
Every home within 1.2 km of a frequent stop is one walk, from the stop to the home (431,100 walks). Results are always reported by trip length (under 300 m, 300–800 m, 800–1,200 m), and places are only compared within one length band, because short walks rarely have any alternative. Rapid transit and high-frequency bus are reported separately.
Walking the other way (home to stop) gives the same answer: for 500 walks of at least 400 m, the mean sun reduction is 14.2% one way and 14.2% the other (correlation 0.990).

title: Methods
text:
Metrics







Metric
Definition




Sun share
metres in the sun on the shortest path ÷ its length


Sun reduction
(sun on shortest − sun on coolest) ÷ sun on shortest


Detour
(coolest length − shortest length) ÷ shortest length


Weighted exposure reduction
(C of shortest − C of coolest) ÷ C of shortest


No cooler alternative
sun reduction below 2% (the break after the spike at 0 in the distribution of 300–1,200 m walks)


Indoor Contribution Index
(1 − Lcoolest ÷ Lshortest, outdoor) × indoor share of the coolest path’s shade (Wen et al. 2025)



Sun reduction and weighted exposure answer different questions: the first is how much sun you can avoid, the second how much the walk’s heat burden falls when shade is valued at θ. With θ around 0.2, avoiding one metre of sun lowers C by only about 0.15–0.2 m, so weighted exposure falls roughly a tenth as much as sun.

title: Methods
text:
Indoor scenarios (University City)
Each mapped entrance is linked to the nearest sidewalk, and passages through a building count as indoor, air-conditioned walking. Three cases are compared: outdoor only, adding the buildings open without a Penn ID, and adding all mapped buildings. The shortest route is always the outdoor one.

How we checked
The five rapid-transit stations with the largest sun reduction were checked by eye on aerial photos (see Results).

Building and tree heights come from the 2022 LiDAR survey, flown before the leaves came out. Building heights agree closely with the city’s own records (median absolute difference 0.5 m over 541,222 buildings); bridges and elevated rail lines are included, so they cast shadows too. Trees cover 17% of the city in the model (the median tree is 15 m tall). Covered walkways and passages through buildings (4.2 km) are always in shade.





University City in the height model: buildings (blue and pink), bridges and other structures (orange) and trees (green).

title: Data
text:
Whose walks
Each walk starts at a stop: any rapid-transit station (Regional Rail, L (Market-Frankford), B (Broad Street) or the T trolley tunnel) or a bus stop with at least 6 buses an hour in one direction between 15:00 and 19:00. Every home within 1.2 km walking distance of such a stop is one walk, 431,100 in all. The other 91,649 homes (17.5%), mostly in the Northeast and Roxborough, have no frequent stop that close.





Homes without a frequent stop within 1.2 km (red).

title: Data
text:
University City
For University City we mapped the entrances and indoor passages of 41 buildings (4.4 km of passages); 10 of them can be entered without a Penn ID. Campus footpaths from OpenStreetMap are added to the sidewalk network there.

title: Data
text:
Known gaps

Outside University City, campus and park paths are missing, so cooler options inside campuses and parks are understated.
Shadows assume clear skies on two summer days; trees are mapped from leaf-off LiDAR and 2018 land cover, buildings from 2022.
Missing or misplaced footprints, newer buildings and temporary objects (parked trains, scaffolding) affect shade locally.
The timetable is one weekday in fall 2026; summer service may differ.

The coolest route is rarely more than a few percent longer. Mean detours stay below 1% in every group, and 95% of coolest walks are at most 0.9%–3.5% longer than the shortest walk, depending on the group.
Rapid-transit walks gain more than bus walks of the same length: stations sit in denser, taller parts of the city where a parallel street in building shade is usually available.
Short walks have no choice. Under 300 m, more than four in five walks have no cooler option.
Weighted exposure falls much less than sun. With θ near 0.2, a metre moved from sun into shade lowers the cost by only 0.2 m; the remaining heat burden of shaded walking is still counted.






Sun reduction by hour, walks of 300–800 m (dynamic θ).




Morning and evening, when shadows are long, offer the most; around 13:00 the sun is high and little shade is left to choose.

Campus = building to building; Station = rapid-transit station to building. * compared with the shortest walk on the outdoor-only network.
Opening the annotated buildings puts about one in five coolest walks indoors and removes another 1.2–2.4 points of sun, without making walks longer. The Indoor Contribution Index stays close to zero (median below 0.001 in absolute value): indoor passages here offer an equally long but cooler option, not a shortcut. This differs from the Dubai stations of Wen et al. (2025), where indoor networks through malls and connected towers make indoor routes real shortcuts. With θ near 0.2–0.3 for most of a 300–1,200 m walk, an indoor metre beats building shade by only about 0.1 m of cost, so indoor routes are chosen mainly when they are already on the way; walks of 800–1,200 m use them about three times as often as walks of 300–800 m.

title: Results
text:
Limitations

Outside University City, campus and park walkways are missing, so cooler options there are understated.
“No cooler option” mixes two cases: no cooler street exists, or one exists but is not worth the detour at the default shade preference.
Shadows are for clear-sky June 21 and August 1; trees from leaf-off LiDAR and 2018 land cover; buildings from 2022.
Indoor passages assume buildings are open and air-conditioned; opening hours and security are not modelled.
